got_right: Random assignment to an op-ed against the respondent's own position versus a placebo article, with the chatbot in both arms, so the op-ed effect is cleanly identified (H1 0.64, 95% CI [0.37, 0.91]).
Tied the attitude result to a behavioural trace in the conversation: op-ed keyword use rose by 16.6 pp (counterargument) and 26.7 pp (supportive), both well above their MDEs.
Reported HC2 intervals, the n lost to missing values (446 to 439) and the underpowered anti-spending subgroup (n=59, interaction p=0.37) without overclaiming.
Open data and a replication script, so the post hoc plan can be audited.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Both arms get the chatbot, so the study cannot say whether the chatbot works as a measurement device or adds persuasion. The title question is untested.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: Placebo + chatbot is the control; the Limitations section concedes the chatbot's contribution cannot be separated.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: Keyword use may be echo of the op-ed rather than adopted belief. Supportive keywords (own side) rose more than counterargument keywords, which fits echoing or topic priming better than persuasion.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: H4 0.267 vs H3 0.166, control means 0.08 and 0.09; no validation against attitudes.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: The certainty effect is barely above the detectable threshold, so its size is uncertain. The anti-spending subgroup is far too small to test moderation.
why_it_did_not_land.evidence: H2 observed/MDE = 1.03 (-5.31 vs 5.15); S1 anti-spending n=59, interaction 0.425, p=0.372.

why_it_did_not_land.detail: No pre-registration and no multiplicity correction; the plan was reconstructed from the replication script. All results are post hoc, and the claim check returned major_revision.
Outcomes were measured right after exposure in one US panel, and only 13% of the sample held the anti-spending position, so durability and generality are unknown.

debates.label: Does the chatbot add persuasion beyond the text?
debates.position_a: Conversational interaction adds persuasive or compliance value beyond static text.
debates.position_b: Chatbot interaction yields superficial engagement; any attitude shift comes from the text and may not last.
debates.what_this_study_says: It cannot tell. The chatbot is in both arms, so the 0.64 effect is attributable to the op-ed and the chatbot's marginal contribution is unidentified. The retrieved works are mostly customer-service or general AI papers, so the debate is only weakly grounded.

briefs.title: Validating conversation keywords against attitudes, with a no-chat arm and delayed follow-up
briefs.question: Do op-ed keywords in chatbot conversations track genuine attitude change, and does the chat add to the op-ed's effect?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses design and measurement: a no-chatbot arm identifies the chatbot's contribution, a pre-chat attitude measure ties keywords to belief change, and a wave 2 tests durability.
briefs.design_sketch: Randomise to op-ed+chatbot, op-ed only, placebo+chatbot, placebo only. Measure attitude and certainty before and immediately after, and again at about 2 weeks. Code keywords with the existing dictionary plus a blinded human or LLM coding of argument adoption versus echo. Test whether keyword use mediates or predicts attitude shift within the op-ed arms.

power_target.basis: H1 MDE 0.3985 at 224/215 per arm; observed 0.638. Because the chat increment is likely smaller than the full effect, consider about 400 per arm.

briefs.title: Chatbot as persuader versus passive measurement
briefs.question: Does the chatbot's conversational role (challenging, neutral, or absent) change attitude shift after the same op-ed?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses design and framing by discriminating between the 'adds value' and 'superficial engagement' positions of D1.
briefs.design_sketch: All participants read the op-ed. Randomise to a chatbot that argues back, a chatbot that only asks neutral questions, or a static comparison task of equal length. Outcome is attitude change at once and at 1 week. If position a holds, the arguing chatbot beats the other two; if position b holds, the arms are equal and the effect decays.

power_target.basis: Chat increment is expected to be at most about half the observed 0.64; the SD of 1.49 from the H1 row gives MDE about 0.29 at 400 per arm.

briefs.title: Oversampling the anti-spending position and varying topic
briefs.question: Does the op-ed plus chatbot effect hold for respondents opposed to the spending position and on other issues?
briefs.why_this_fixes_the_failure: Addresses sample and power: the anti-spending group (n=59) could not test moderation (interaction p=0.37).
briefs.design_sketch: Recruit equal numbers of pro- and anti-spending respondents and add a second, unrelated policy topic. Use the same op-ed versus placebo contrast, with the chatbot in both arms. Estimate the treatment by position and treatment by topic interactions.
briefs.moderator_or_condition: Prior position (pro vs anti spending) and issue topic

power_target.basis: Anti-spending effect of 0.23 (SE 0.454 at n=59); detecting 0.23 needs about 650 per cell at SD 1.49, so 250 per arm detects only about 0.35 within a subgroup. Size to the interaction as the target.

verdict: A follow-up is worth running. The op-ed effect is solid (H1 1.6x MDE), but the study cannot answer its titular question about the chatbot, because every arm had one. Run advance_design first: it adds no-chat arms, validates the keyword measure against pre/post attitudes and adds a delayed wave, which resolves the main design and measurement gaps. The literature offers only a thin debate, with mostly off-topic retrieved works, so ground the theory in persuasion and LLM-dialogue papers before preregistering.
